Official results won't be declared until Wednesday, Oct. 21. Also at home Saturday, Oct. 17 was former mayor and challenger Walter Cobb where he too awaited election results. Incumbent Surinderpal Rathor will remain mayor of Williams Lake for a second term following this year’s municipal election. According to preliminary results that were shared approximately 50 minutes after voting closed 8 p.m. at Marie Sharpe Elementary School, Rathor was identified as the successful candidate against challenger and former mayor Walt Cobb. Rathor was elected mayor in 2022 after serving as a city councillor for more than 20 years. Rathor was at home with family, friends and supporters eagerly awaiting for the results to come in, shortly after which he shared a Facebook post. “Thank you for trusting me to continue serving as your mayor. Together we can!” In 2014 and 2018 Rathor was defeated by Cobb for the top position. Preliminary results which won’t be made official until Wednesday, Oct. 21, show Rathor securing 2,116 votes (913 advance and 1,203 general) compared to Cobb’s total of 1,026 (530 advance and 496 general). Councillor incumbents Scott Nelson and Michael Moses were also successfully re-elected. New faces set to take up a councillor seat include Ruth Lloyd and Nathan Wiebe with past city councillors Jason Ryll and Paul French returning. City of Williams Lake chief election officer Ross Coupé said there were a total of 3,182 ballots cast. Preliminary results show incumbent Sheila Boehm unsuccessful in her re-election efforts. Coun. Joan Flaspohler, Jazmyn Lyons and Angie Delainey did not seek re-election.

items.title: [Fast Company] As a domestic car sales slump continues, China’s automakers lean on exports
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

China’s passenger car exports surged 64% in September from the same month in 2025, an industry association reported Monday, as Chinese automakers increasingly focus on exports to drive growth amid sluggish domestic sales.

China exported around 919,000 passenger vehicles in September, lifted by overseas demand for plug-in hybrids and pure electric vehicles, data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers showed. In the first nine months of 2026, China exported over 7.1 million passenger cars, up more than 70% from the same period last year.

Meanwhile, domestic passenger car sales in China fell for most of the year as automakers faced weaker consumer confidence at home and scaled-back government subsidies. They fell 27% year over year in September to over 1.6 million units, according to the association.

China is the world’s largest vehicle exporter, but is facing increasing skepticism from trade partners who fear it’s undermining their domestic industries and trade balance.

The European Union is capping Chinese hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 a year, officials say.

Chinese car sales grow in regions including Europe

In recent months, Chinese automakers have more aggressively targeted rapid growth in overseas markets such as Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and Africa. Canada is also opening its doors to Chinese EV exports under a tariff cut deal with China.

The industry increasingly relies on overseas markets for sales and profit growth as players seek to offset weakness in the domestic market, analyst Stephen Chan of S&P Global Ratings said.

Consultancy AlixPartners and some auto analysts expect Chinese automakers to export nearly or around 10 million vehicles globally in 2026.

In Europe, Chinese automakers are increasingly challenging the European auto industry with lower costs and prices. AlixPartners’ analysis found, for example, that a Chinese-branded EV costs around $20,000 to produce, compared with $31,000 for a European equivalent.

EU to cap Chinese hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 annually

The EU has already imposed higher tariffs on pure electric vehicles from China, prompting Chinese carmakers to export more hybrid vehicles. Recent policy discussions have focused on the rapid rise in sales of Chinese hybrids in Europe.

Chinese automakers captured around 12% of Europe’s new-car market in August and accounted for one in four hybrid sales in the region, said a research note by Deutsche Bank.

Amid growing pressure on the EU to rebalance trade with China, EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič said Friday that the two sides had reached an interim deal that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc.

The agreement sets an annual import quota of 350,000 hybrid vehicles made in China, including plug-in hybrids, two senior EU officials said Monday. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity under European Commission policy.

Starting as early as December, customs authorities across the 27-nation bloc will coordinate monitoring of these imports and halt further shipments once the annual quota is reached, one official said. The limit excludes cars made in Europe by Chinese companies.

Analysts said protectionist measures would likely continue to cloud Chinese automakers’ overseas outlook.

An import cap on Chinese hybrid cars would likely disrupt the highly profitable vehicle export growth that Chinese automakers recently enjoyed in the European market, Deutsche Bank analysts said.

“You can’t expect BYD or the other OEMs [original equipment manufacturers] to export too many cars without facing tariffs or pushbacks from the foreign governments,” Xiao Feng, head of Hong Kong and China industrials research at investment group CITIC CLSA, told reporters recently.

Geopolitics is the biggest challenge to BYD’s overseas expansion, executive vice president Stella Li, who leads the Chinese EV giant’s global growth, acknowledged at an event this month.

BYD has therefore been expanding overseas production, including setting up plants in Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, and Hungary, she told the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore.

More overseas production limits impact from trade curbs

Chinese automakers will likely continue to expand overseas production to reduce exposure to tariffs and other risks, said Ming Lee, head of Greater China automotive and industrial research at BofA Global Research, a unit of Bank of America.

“More and more volume will be made locally,” he said.

Meanwhile, the U.S. has effectively shut Chinese EVs out of its market with hefty tariffs. President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during Xi’s state visit to Washington last month yielded no deal on access for Chinese EVs.

Experts say continued political uncertainty likely makes the U.S. market a lower priority for Chinese automakers.

items.title: [Fast Company] What happens when people have to jump in to clean up AI’s mess?
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.

But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.

What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

Human in the loop explained.

The success paradox

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance—rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ironies of automation”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.

This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

The accountability problem

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility, and capability can begin to separate.

Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

The measurement problem

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.

The governance problem

Organizational governance—defining roles and responsibilities—is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?

In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.

For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

Murugan Anandarajan is a professor of decision sciences and management information systems at Drexel University.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] Meshtastic Offline GPS Tracking: Save Your Route Without a Phone
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A Meshtastic device can send its GPS position over the air, but that is not the same as keeping a track on the device itself. In the standard setup I was using, disconnecting the phone meant the node continued broadcasting its location without saving a local history for later. I wanted something simple: take a node out for a walk, leave the phone disconnected, and download the route when I got home. So I modified the Meshtastic firmware to add on-device GPS location caching. I have this running on a SenseCAP T1000E and a Heltec T096. Both remain Meshtastic nodes, with their normal communication functions, but now they can also record a route independently of the phone. Key Takeaways The custom firmware records GPS points on the node without a connected phone. A 500-point cache provides roughly eight hours of recording at one point per minute. Reconnect to Meshtastic to load saved positions, then export them as GPX. Clearing app history does not clear the tracker cache; use the device controls to remove saved points. Table of ContentsWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware AddsUsing the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000ESyncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic AppExporting Your Route as a GPX FileClearing the Tracker CacheInstalling the Firmware and Exploring the CodeWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware Adds Meshtastic is open source, and its module system gives you a useful way to add your own functionality without creating an entirely separate application. My modification adds a local cache for GPS points, controls for starting and stopping recording, and a way to replay those saved positions into the Meshtastic app. The basic workflow is: Start tracking on the device. Go walking or travelling without a connected phone. Reconnect to the Meshtastic app afterward. Let the saved positions populate the map. Export the track to GPX if you want to use it elsewhere. The device still sends position updates over the air as normal. Local recording is an additional function, not a replacement for Meshtastic communication. You can still receive messages and hear the usual notification sounds while recording your route. 500 points, recorded once per minute In this build, I set the cache capacity to 500 location points. With automatic recording every minute, that gives you roughly eight hours of tracking capacity, provided the device has a GPS location to save. That figure describes the number of points the cache can hold, not a battery-life measurement. You can also build up a collection of points across separate outings. One of my test devices had 205 points collected during experiments over about a month, while the other contained routes from several days of walking. Using the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096 The T096 still has the familiar Meshtastic screens. I added one extra page for the tracker, showing whether recording is on or off and how many points are cached. For example, the display can show tracking switched off with 205 of 500 points cached. Stopping recording does not remove those points. They remain available to download later. To start recording: Navigate to the tracker screen. Long-press the button to open its menu. Select Start Tracking. Check that the tracker screen changes to Tracking On. With tracking enabled, the firmware saves a location every minute when a GPS position is available. The cached-point counter increases as points are recorded. A count of 205, for instance, becomes 206 after the next successful recording. To stop, open the menu again and select Stop Tracking. This stops the extra local recording function. The node continues doing its normal Meshtastic work, including sending positions according to its configuration. The same menu also includes Clear Cache, but save that until you have downloaded or exported anything you want to keep. Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000E The T1000E does not have a screen, so I implemented the tracker controls through its button. The idea is to make it useful on its own, without needing to pull out a phone just to start a walk. Button action Tracker function One press Save the current location to the cache. Two presses Start or stop automatic recording every minute. Three presses Clear the cached locations. A double press starts recording with an audible beep. While recording, the device beeps every minute as it records. Double-press again to stop. The single-press action is handy when you just want to record where you are right now, rather than run continuous tracking. It writes that current location into the same cache. These shortcuts belong to this custom firmware. They are not instructions for the standard T1000E firmware. Syncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic App Once you return, connect to the device through the Meshtastic app as usual. There is no separate tracker app required for this part. Scan for nearby devices in the app's connection screen. Select the node you used for recording. Open that node's details and its Position history. Allow the connection to finish and the cached positions to arrive. The position history may initially look empty. In my demonstration, the connection indicator was orange while connecting, then turned green. Once connected, the saved positions started arriving and the route filled in on the map. The saved points populate the map after the node reconnects. On my T096, the downloaded history included driving routes as well as the walking route I use regularly. Connecting to the T1000E brought in its own saved points from several days of walking. Apparently, I do quite a lot of walking! Deleting app history does not clear the device This is an important distinction: the app's position history and the device's cache are separate. I deleted the position history in the app, disconnected, and connected again. The device replayed the saved positions, and the route appeared again. The points were still on the node. So, if a route returns after you delete it from the phone, that is expected. To remove the source of that replay, you need to clear the cache on the tracker itself. Exporting Your Route as a GPX File Once the positions are in the Meshtastic app, you can export them as a GPX file and open the result in another mapping application. I exported a test track, gave it a name, then opened it through the file browser in GPX Viewer. The same route appeared there, this time drawn over its map. The process is straightforward: Wait for the cached positions to finish loading into Meshtastic. Use the position-history export option to save a GPX file. Give the file a name. Open it in GPX Viewer or another application that supports GPX. I also included a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat. It provides another way to export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app. The repository documentation explains that option. Clearing the Tracker Cache After saving your route, you can clear the device's cached positions so they no longer replay into the app. T1000E: Press the button three times. T096: Long-press to open the tracker menu, select Clear Cache, and confirm that you want to clear it. On the T096, the counter returns to 0 of 500. After I cleared the cache and reconnected, the old saved route no longer arrived. A current location could still appear, but that was a fresh position rather than the previous cached history. If you want to remove the route from both places, clear the app's history as well as the device's cache. Export anything important first. Installing the Firmware and Exploring the Code I put the firmware, source changes, and instructions in the tracker-firmware GitHub repository. It includes builds for the T096 and T1000E, device-control documentation, installation notes, and the Windows export tool. Before flashing, back up your Meshtastic configuration and export your keys. Do that first, before changing the firmware. For the demonstrated devices, installation uses the familiar flashing-mode and drag-and-drop process: Back up your existing configuration and keys. Download the firmware file that matches your device. Put the device into flashing mode. Drag and drop the matching firmware file onto the device's flashing drive. The flashing instructions shown for the T096 use two presses of Reset to make the drive appear. For the T1000E, hold the button while connecting the charging cable. Follow the repository's device-specific instructions rather than assuming that every Meshtastic board flashes the same way. How the modification fits into Meshtastic I used Meshtastic 2.8.1 for the demonstrated build. The tracker changes can also be incorporated into another firmware version and compiled, rather than being tied only to that build. The source changes are concentrated in four files. Part of the work changes the button-handling thread, because the tracker needs those additional button actions. The rest uses Meshtastic's optional add-on modules, which provide a place for custom functionality to run inside the firmware. I also compiled an ESP32-S3 version, mentioning Heltec V3 and V4 hardware as additional targets. That is separate from the hands-on T096 and T1000E examples here, so check the available files and instructions for your particular board. The LoRaWAN edition is a separate project I have a similar tracker project for the T1000E LoRaWAN edition, with comparable single-press and double-press controls. That project is aimed at LoRaWAN rather than Meshtastic. Do not confuse the LoRaWAN-edition firmware with the Meshtastic tracker build. There are supporting write-ups and architecture diagrams on the resource hub, but the firmware must match the device edition and the system you intend to use. What I like about this modification is how little it changes the everyday experience. It is still a Meshtastic node. It simply remembers where it has been, so you can take it out on its own and bring the route back afterward. Try the Offline GPS Tracker Firmware Get the T096 and T1000E firmware builds, source changes, installation instructions, and Windows GPX export tool. Get the Firmware on GitHub Frequently Asked Questions Does offline tracking stop the device from working as a Meshtastic node? No. The modification adds local location caching while retaining normal Meshtastic communication, including position broadcasts and message reception. Does the tracker save a point every minute without a GPS location? The automatic recording interval is one minute, but the device needs a GPS position available to save a location point. Why do deleted tracks return when I reconnect? Deleting position history in the app does not remove the points cached on the device. Reconnecting allows the node to replay them. Clear the device cache if you no longer want those saved positions to return. Can I export tracks without the Meshtastic phone app? Yes. The repository includes a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat that can export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app.
